posts.quote: THE JAR LID WOULD NOT BUDGE UNTIL DAD RAN IT UNDER HOT WATER, AND THE WHOLE KITCHEN WAITED FOR THE POP.
posts.caption: The pickle jar lid would not move, and everybody in the family had already tried. Mom gave it a go with a dish towel, my sister tried it with a rubber band, and I held the jar against my stomach and grunted. Then Dad came in from the garage, ran the lid under the hot tap for about twenty seconds, and gave it one quiet twist. Pop. The whole kitchen had been holding its breath, and now we let it out together. He set the jar on the table without a word and went back to whatever he had been working on.
posts.first: Dad never explained the hot water trick, and I didn't learn why it worked until I was grown. I just knew that when a jar was stuck, he was the one who got called. I think he liked that more than he let on.

posts.quote: THE BOOT SCRAPER BESIDE THE FRONT STEPS WAS THERE FOR A REASON, AND MOM ENFORCED IT.
posts.caption: Every front step in the neighborhood had an iron boot scraper bolted beside it, a little black blade on two short legs. You dragged each boot across it, left then right, and then wiped them on the mat for good measure. Mom could tell from the kitchen whether you had done it, and she never needed to look. Mud in the spring, slush in the winter, and the same rule all year. The scraper never changed, because nobody ever thought of a reason to replace it. A few of those iron blades are still standing beside old front steps, doing the same job.
posts.first: Ours was set in the concrete so firmly that my father said the house would fall before it did. I wiped my boots on it every day for eighteen years. I still do it without thinking, even on a clean sidewalk.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the piano tuner)
posts.quote: THE PIANO TUNER / A TUNING FORK, A FELT STRIP, AND AN HOUR OF ONE NOTE
posts.caption: The piano tuner came once a year, always on a weekday, and he carried everything in a worn leather case. He lifted the lid, took out a felt strip and a little steel fork, and struck one note. Then he struck it again, and again, for what felt like an hour. We kids were told not to touch the piano and not to ask when he would be done. When he finally played a full chord, the whole parlor sounded like it had been rinsed clean. He packed up his case, took his check, and left us with a piano that sounded better than any of us deserved.
posts.first: Ours was a 1920s upright that had belonged to my grandmother, and it never held a tune for more than a month. The tuner always blamed the radiator. I think it was just old and stubborn, and I loved it for that.

posts.quote: GRANDPA PEELED APPLES WITH HIS POCKETKNIFE IN ONE LONG CURL, AND HE NEVER ONCE BROKE IT.
posts.caption: Grandpa carried a pocketknife in his right pocket, and on fall afternoons it came out for the apples. He would sit on the back steps with a bowl in his lap and take the skin off in one long ribbon, never lifting the blade. The curl hung down past his knee and he held it up like a prize. We watched him do it a dozen times and never once saw it break. When he finally handed each of us a slice, it came off the knife with a little flick of his thumb. I have peeled apples every way there is since, and none of them tasted like those.
posts.first: I tried to copy him one October with a paring knife and ended up with about forty tiny pieces of peel. He laughed so hard he had to set his bowl down. He told me it took him ten years to get it right, and I believed him.

posts.quote: The good towels were for company, and in forty years company never once showed up.
posts.first: Ours had a little pink border and a tag still on one corner. They stayed folded on the linen shelf until I moved out. When I cleaned out the house years later, they were still exactly where she had put them.

posts.quote: THE THERMOMETER OUTSIDE THE KITCHEN WINDOW RAN THE WHOLE FAMILY'S DAY.
posts.caption: The first thing anyone did in the morning was check the thermometer outside the kitchen window. It was a tin one with a red line, nailed to the frame, with a little crust of paint on one side. Dad read it over his coffee and announced the number like a hired hand reporting for work. That number settled everything: whether the car would start, how many layers you wore, and whether anybody was going sledding. If it said ten, you did not argue. If it said sixty in February, the porch chairs came out and the neighbors were told.
posts.first: My mother tapped the glass every morning, in case it was stuck. It never was, but she tapped it anyway. I tap my own window now when it's cold out, and I could not tell you why.

posts.quote: DAD'S WORK GLOVES WENT ALL THE WAY TO YOUR ELBOWS, AND PUTTING THEM ON MADE YOU FEEL LIKE YOU HAD A JOB.
posts.caption: Dad's work gloves lived on the shelf by the back door, stiff as boards from years of use. When he wasn't looking, you slipped them on and your hands disappeared all the way up your forearms. You clapped them together and they made a dull, important sound. For a few minutes you were a man with a job and a truck and somewhere to be. You dragged a rake across the garage floor like it was a day's wages. Then Dad came around the corner, took one look, and said nothing, because he knew exactly what you were doing.
posts.first: Mine were his old pair, cracked across the knuckles and smelling like motor oil and cut grass. He kept them for years after he bought a new pair, and I never asked why. I think I know now.

posts.quote: THE WINDOW DRESSER / A BARE MANNEQUIN, A BOX OF PINS, AND A NEW STORY EVERY MONDAY
posts.caption: The big department store downtown changed its front windows every Monday morning. A man with a pincushion on his wrist worked behind a paper screen so nobody could peek. By lunchtime the mannequins had new outfits, a new backdrop, and sometimes a little painted snow. People stopped on the sidewalk on their way to work just to see what had changed. Kids pressed their noses against the glass and pointed at things they would never be able to afford. It was theater with no tickets, and the whole street got a front-row seat.
posts.first: My mother used to walk us past the windows on the way to the bus stop, even when it was out of our way. She never bought a thing there. She just liked to see what the man had come up with that week.

posts.quote: THE FIRST WARM DAY OF MARCH, EVERY KID LEFT HIS COAT IN THE GRASS, AND EVERY MOTHER WENT BACK FOR IT.
posts.caption: March finally gave us one warm afternoon, and every coat on the block came off at once. They landed on lawns, over fences, and across the handlebars of bicycles. We ran around in our shirtsleeves like we had been let out of jail, even though the ground was still half mud. The sun lasted about three hours. By supper the wind had come back and the whole neighborhood was shivering. Mothers walked out in their aprons and collected coats like they were gathering the laundry, and nobody said I told you so. Well, almost nobody.
posts.first: My mother kept a count of how many times she went back for my jacket, and she once told me the record was four in one week. I can still see her crossing the lawn with it over her arm, shaking her head. She never once raised her voice.

posts.quote: THE STEP STOOL BY THE BATHROOM SINK WAS HOW YOU FINALLY GOT TO SEE YOURSELF IN THE MIRROR.
posts.caption: The step stool lived beside the bathroom sink, painted white and chipped at the corners. It was how you brushed your teeth, washed your face, and had your hair parted before school. One day you stepped up on it and finally saw the top of your own head in the mirror. Mom used it to reach the top shelf of the medicine cabinet and the box of bobby pins. Then one year you realized you could see over the sink without it. Nobody mentioned it, but it stayed there by the sink, waiting for the next kid.
posts.first: Ours had two steps and a rubber foot that was always coming loose. My sister and I wore the paint off the top step with our shoes. When my own son got tall enough to need it, I found I had never once thrown it away.
